newsitem.title: USA: Mexico's Ortiz sees no grounds for peso complaints.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Ortiz sees no grounds for peso complaints.

text.p: Mexican Finance Secretary Guillermo Ortiz dismissed on Wednesday criticism that Mexico's peso currency may be overvalued.

"I don't think there are any grounds to sustain that the peso is being manipulated. The Central Bank has not intervened in the exchange market," Ortiz, who is attending the International Monetary Fund/World Bank annual meeting, told Reuters Financial Television.
Ortiz was reacting to recent comments made by U.S. economist Rudiger Dornbusch, an MIT professor who predicted the disastruous peso devaluation of December, 1994.

Dornbusch, speaking earlier this week at a conference in the Mexican resort of Cancun, warned that the peso would be headed for trouble unless the government starts moving towards what he called "a real exchange rate policy."

Ortiz said he understood that the German-born academic's argument was that Mexico's central bank had manipulated the exchange rate through its monetary policy, causing it to appreciate against the dollar.
"As you may have observed, (domestic) interest rates have been coming down, so I think that the Bank of Mexico is not doing that," he added.
According to Ortiz, whose predecessor Jaime Serra Puche was unseated by the peso's massive fall, there were no concerns about the present exchange rate.
He did concede, however, that some people may worry that the Mexican currency could over-appreciate in the future.
"By definition, if you have a floating exchange rate system, if you have a market-determined exchange rate, then it cannot be over or undervalued over a period of time," he said.
The peso has barely moved in nominal terms this year. The most-watched 48-hour contract was trading at around 7.52 to the dollar earlier Wednesday, against 7.49 a year ago.
Such stability, despite Mexico's consumer price index rising about 30 percent, has fueled concerns that the peso will eventually strengthen, blunting the competitive advantage of Mexican exports.

The peso plunged to about seven to the dollar early last year from around 3.45 in December, 1994, after the Mexican government failed in an attempt to devalue the currency by only 20 percent in domestic terms.
